pub.answer_rationale: The sentence has one independent clause with the subject 'Her early fieldwork' and needs a single main verb 'laid' to complete it without inserting an unnecessary comma, semicolon, or coordinating conjunction that would create a fragment or faulty structure.
pub.evidence_span: Her early fieldwork, conducted in the temperate rainforests of the Pacific Northwest, ______ the foundation for her later claims
pub.explanation: 이 문장은 'Her early fieldwork, conducted in the temperate rainforests of the Pacific Northwest,'라는 주어(삽입구 포함)와 'the foundation for her later claims...'라는 목적어를 하나의 독립절로 연결해야 한다. 정답 'laid'는 단순히 문장의 본동사로 기능하여 하나의 완전한 절을 이룬다. 'laid, which became'은 관계절을 이상하게 삽입해 문장 구조를 어색하게 만들고 의미가 통하지 않는다(무엇이 became 되었는지 불명확). 'laid; it became'은 세미콜론 뒤에 새로운 독립절을 넣어 두 개의 절을 만들지만, 원래 문장에는 목적어 'the foundation...'이 이어져야 하므로 이 구조는 문장을 어색하게 끊어버려 뒤의 목적어와 연결되지 않는다. 'laid, and it became'도 마찬가지로 등위접속사로 불필요한 절을 만들어 원래 의도한 단순 서술 구조를 깨뜨린다. 따라서 정답은 D번이다.
pub.explanation_en: This sentence must connect the subject (including its inserted phrase), "Her early fieldwork, conducted in the temperate rainforests of the Pacific Northwest," with the object, "the foundation for her later claims...," in a single independent clause. The correct answer "laid" simply works as the main verb of the sentence and forms one complete clause. "Laid, which became" awkwardly inserts a relative clause, which muddles the sentence structure and the meaning (it is unclear what became what). "Laid; it became" puts a new independent clause after the semicolon and makes two clauses, but the original sentence needs the object "the foundation..." to follow, so this structure breaks the sentence and leaves the later object disconnected. "Laid, and it became" likewise creates an unnecessary clause with a coordinating conjunction and breaks the simple predicate structure originally intended. So the answer is D.
options: laid, which became
laid; it became
laid, and it became
laid

difficultyReasons: laid가 타동사이므로 목적어(the foundation)가 바로 뒤에 와야 한다는 단일 문법 규칙만 확인하면 됨(1단계)
동사-목적어 관계라는 비교적 명확한 문법 관계만 파악하면 되어 미묘함이 낮음
세 오답 모두 laid 뒤에 목적어를 두지 않고 별도의 절로 처리한다는 공통 오류를 공유해 정답과 구조적으로 유사함
별도의 자료 해석 없이 문장 자체의 문법 구조만 보면 됨

distractors.matches: 뒤에 나오는 'became the foundation'이라는 의미와 연결되어 그럴듯해 보임
distractors.plausibleBecause: 관계대명사 which로 절을 연결해 부가 설명을 추가하는 자연스러운 문장 구조처럼 보임
distractors.whyWrong: laid 뒤에 목적어(the foundation)가 이미 필요한 자리인데 which became이 삽입되면 laid가 목적어를 갖지 못해 문장이 비문법적이 됨(laid는 타동사로 목적어 필요)

distractors.matches: 뒤 절 'it became the foundation'이 앞 내용과 의미상 이어짐
distractors.plausibleBecause: 세미콜론으로 두 개의 독립절을 연결하는 것은 문법적으로 흔한 패턴
distractors.whyWrong: 세미콜론을 쓰려면 앞부분도 독립절이어야 하는데 'Her early fieldwork... laid'는 목적어가 빠진 불완전한 절이라 독립절이 아님

distractors.matches: 뒤 절 'it became the foundation'과 의미가 연결됨
distractors.plausibleBecause: and로 두 절을 등위 연결하는 것도 흔한 문장 형태
distractors.whyWrong: and로 연결하려면 앞절도 완전한 독립절이어야 하는데 laid 뒤에 목적어가 없어 불완전함

issues: 선택지 B가 유일하게 목적어(the foundation...)와 문법적으로 연결되는 단순 동사 형태이므로 정답 판정 자체는 타당하나, 이 문항은 사실상 '어떤 선택지가 문장을 완전한 하나의 절로 만드는가'만 묻고 있어 난이도가 매우 낮고 SAT boundaries 유형(구두점/절 경계) 문제로서의 변별력이 부족하다.

해설에서 '무엇이 became 되었는지 불명확하다'는 설명은 다소 부정확하다. 'laid, which became'은 문법적으로는 constructed될 수 있으나('which'가 'the foundation'을 가리켜 became이 이어지는 구조), 실제로는 뒤에 이어지는 목적어 'the foundation for her later claims'와 충돌하여 문장이 완성되지 않는 것이 핵심 문제이다. 해설이 이 핵심 문법적 결함(관계절이 원래 목적어를 대체해버려 문장이 성립하지 않음)을 명확히 짚지 못하고 '의미가 통하지 않는다'는 모호한 표현에 그친다.

pub.question: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?

pub.explanation: 첫 단락은 식물의 변화가 '더 나은 땅이 멀지 않다'는 희망을 준다고 기록하며 새 식물을 모았다고 적는다. 8월 7일 기록에서는 말들이 먹이와 물 부족으로 고생한다는 걱정으로 바뀐다. 따라서 B가 맞다. A는 적대적인 사람이 없고, C는 짐이 가볍다고 했으며, D는 목적지에 도착하지 않았으므로 틀리다.
pub.explanation_en: The first paragraph records that the change in vegetation gives hope that "better land is not far off" and notes that new plants were collected. The August 7 entry shifts to worry that the horses are suffering from a lack of feed and water. Therefore, B is correct. A fails because there are no hostile people, C fails because the loads are said to be light, and D fails because they have not reached their destination.
options: It moves from fear of hostile people to relief at finding fresh provisions.
It moves from hopeful notes on new plants to concern about the suffering horses.
It moves from complaints about heavy loads to praise for the fertile country.
It moves from distress over lost horses to joy at reaching their destination.
pub.passage:
The botanical productions of the hills seemed also to undergo a considerable change, indicating, as we would fain hope, that a better country is not far off. Several new plants were acquired today, some of which were very beautiful. Our course made good was N. 71. E., distance thirteen miles and a half.

August 7.--The horses suffered much from want of food and water; but it is absolutely necessary to proceed and get into a better country with all the expedition which we are capable of using, and which the nature of this country will allow. It is some consolation to us that the horses are but lightly loaded, by reason of our not being now encumbered with much provisions, and are consequently enabled to travel farther and better.

sourceText.author: Oxley, John
sourceText.work: Journals of Two Expeditions into the Interior of New South Wales

pub.question: Which choice best describes the shift that occurs in the text?

pub.explanation: 처음에는 꽃봉오리가 아직 초록색이고 줄기가 자란다는 사실을 담담하게 관찰한다. 이후 'grow lovely', 'Delicate tints', 'charming flowers', 'delightful fragrance' 같은 표현이 이어지며 감탄하는 어조로 바뀐다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B, C, D는 실망·걱정·무관심을 말하지만 글은 점점 기쁨을 드러낸다.
pub.explanation_en: At first the text calmly observes that the buds are still green and the stems are growing. It then turns to an admiring tone with expressions such as "grow lovely," "Delicate tints," "charming flowers," and "delightful fragrance." So the answer is A. B, C, and D describe disappointment, worry, and indifference, but the text increasingly shows delight.
options: From plain notes on green buds to delighted praise of the blossoms
From eager hope for spring to disappointment at a late, cold spring
From scientific detachment about plants to anxious worry about frost
From gloomy description of winter to bored indifference toward flowers
pub.passage:
The flower clusters are nearly ready to bloom, but the buds are still green. The tall stem has lifted them up into the air and sunlight, and, although the air is still cold, they continue to grow.

Soon the green buds undergo a change. The topmost one on each flower cluster softens to a tender blue or pink.

The green buds grow lovely as they stand on their stems in the sun. Delicate tints steal over them, the green color fades away, and many colors take its place.

They open into charming flowers and give forth a delightful fragrance.
pub.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?

pub.explanation: 필자는 처음에 대부분이 콘스탄티노플에 질렸으며 관광은 조금이면 충분하다고 지친 듯 말한다. 이후 짧게 머물기에는 나쁘지 않다며 호텔 값, 식료품, 집세를 차분히 따지는 실용적 평가로 넘어가므로 B가 정답이다. A는 처음부터 열의가 없었으므로 틀렸고, C의 향수와 D의 두려움은 지문에 드러나지 않는다.
pub.explanation_en: At first the writer says wearily that most people are sick of Constantinople and that a little sightseeing is enough. The writer then shifts to a calm, practical appraisal, saying it is not bad for a short stay and weighing hotel prices, groceries, and rent, so B is the answer. A is wrong because there was no enthusiasm to begin with, and the nostalgia in C and the fear in D do not appear in the text.
options: From eager enthusiasm to bitter disappointment.
From weary dismissal to practical appraisal.
From scholarly detachment to fond nostalgia.
From playful humor to fearful alarm.
pub.passage: I fancy we are most of us tired of Constantinople. To me it is a place where a little sight-seeing goes a long way. Our gallant captain, on the contrary, tells me that he could put in three months here very well. As it is, there are about 2,000 English here, to say nothing of naturalized Greeks and Maltese. I suppose Constantinople is not a bad place for a short residence. The hotels are good, and in some you may have a bedroom for four francs a day. Provisions are not dear, but house-rent is very expensive. The population of the place is dense, at which I wonder, as Constantinople seems to me the most unhealthy city I have ever seen.

sourceText.author: Ritchie, J. Ewing (James Ewing)
sourceText.work: Cities of the Dawn Naples - Athens - Pompeii - Constantinople - Smyrna - Jaffa - Jerusalem - Alexandria - Cairo - Marseilles - Avignon - Lyons - Dijon

pub.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?

pub.explanation: 화자는 집에 오자마자 다른 누구보다 먼저 로티를 찾아가 그녀가 마음에 바라던 모든 것이라고 말한다. 또 밤늦게까지 그녀 곁에 머물며 지난날과 미래를 이야기했다고 서술한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. 의심, 짜증, 죄책감을 보여 주는 표현은 지문에 없으므로 B, C, D는 틀리다.
pub.explanation_en: As soon as he gets home, the narrator goes to see Lottie before anyone else and says she is everything he had hoped for. He also says he stayed by her side late into the night talking about the past and the future. Therefore, A is the answer. B, C, and D are wrong because the text has no expressions showing doubt, irritation, or guilt.
options: Deep affection and delight in her company
Polite respect mixed with quiet doubt
Mild irritation at her emotional display
Guilty unease about his long absence
pub.passage: When I arrived at home I of course went to see Lottie before talking with any one else. I found my darling all that heart could wish. She was more beautiful, more charming in my eyes than ever. The large, dreamy blue eyes were swimming in tears of joy as I held her to my glad heart, and I saw a look of love that satisfied me that I was the possessor of a treasure of great value. I lingered by my darling’s side until late at night. Every little trifling incident was described--the days of old were alluded to and discussed, while the present and future came in for a full share.
pub.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Lottie?

pub.explanation: 전반부에서 그는 소년 같은 기운을 되찾고 도시 불빛을 신드바드의 '다이아몬드 계곡'에 비유하며 자신의 명성이 반짝이기 시작했을지 모른다고 들뜬다. 그러나 집에 들어서자 아내가 자기 이름을 말하다가 어색하게 침묵하는 것을 보고, 자신에 대한 이야기였거나 들으면 안 되는 이야기였음을 느낀다. 따라서 희망찬 들뜸에서 불안한 의심으로 바뀌는 B가 정답이다. C의 분노나 대결, D의 깊은 슬픔은 지문에 나타나지 않는다.
pub.explanation_en: In the first half, he regains a boyish energy and compares the city lights to Sinbad's "valley of diamonds," excitedly thinking his fame may have begun to sparkle. But when he enters the house, he sees his wife trail off awkwardly as she says his name and senses that she was talking about him, or about something he was not meant to hear. Therefore, B, a shift from hopeful elation to uneasy suspicion, is the answer. The angry confrontation in C and the deep grief in D do not appear in the text.
options: From gloomy doubt to sudden, confident triumph.
From hopeful elation to uneasy suspicion.
From calm description to angry confrontation.
From playful humor to deep, lasting grief.
pub.passage:
Once in the fresh air again he promptly recovered his boyish spirits. The light flying scud had already effaced the first rising stars; the lower creeping sea-fog had already blotted out the western shore and sea; but below him to the east the glittering lights of the city seemed to start up with a new, mysterious, and dazzling brilliancy. It was the valley of diamonds that Sindbad saw lying almost at his feet! Perhaps somewhere there the light of his own fame and fortune was already beginning to twinkle!

He returned to his humble roof joyous and inspired. As he entered the hall he heard his wife's voice and his own name mentioned, followed by that awkward, meaningless silence on his entrance which so plainly indicated either that he had been the subject of conversation or that it was not for his ears.
pub.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?

pub.explanation: 화자는 해가 지기 전부터 어둠이 좁은 수로에 스며들었다고 묘사한다. 물살은 빠르게 흘렀지만 강둑에는 말없는 정적이 앉아 있었다는 대비로 섬뜩한 고요함을 드러낸다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. A의 사람들, B의 경사, C의 침식은 구절의 의미가 아니다.
pub.explanation_en: The speaker describes how darkness had crept into the narrow channel even before sunset. The current ran swiftly, yet a dumb stillness sat on the banks, and this contrast conveys an eerie quiet. Therefore, the answer is D. The people in A, the steepness in B, and the erosion in C are not what the phrase means.
options: were crowded with people waiting silently
were too steep for the boat to approach
were slowly being worn away by the current
were eerily silent and still
pub.passage: Eight miles meant nearly three hours’ steaming for us, and I could also see suspicious ripples at the upper end of the reach. Nevertheless, I was annoyed beyond expression at the delay, and most unreasonably, too, since one night more could not matter much after so many months. As we had plenty of wood, and caution was the word, I brought up in the middle of the stream. The reach was narrow, straight, with high sides like a railway cutting. The dusk came gliding into it long before the sun had set. The current ran smooth and swift, but a dumb immobility sat on the banks.

pub.explanation: 필자는 아기의 울음이 이성의 노력에도 몇 시간 동안 자신을 비참하게 만든다고 말한다. 또 망원경으로 큰 소년들이 작은 아이를 괴롭히는 장면을 보고 이성도 용기도 남지 않은 듯했다고 고백한다. 따라서 이 구절은 흔한 고통스러운 장면에 감정적으로 압도되는 상태를 뜻하므로 D가 정답이다. A와 B는 신체적 약함으로, C는 나이로 잘못 해석했다.
pub.explanation_en: The writer says that a baby's cry makes him miserable for hours despite the efforts of reason. He also confesses that when he saw bigger boys bullying a small child through a telescope, he seemed to have no reason or courage left. The phrase therefore means being emotionally overwhelmed by common painful sights, so the answer is D. A and B wrongly interpret it as physical weakness, and C wrongly interprets it as age.
options: physically ill from a lack of rest and food.
unable to lift heavy objects in daily work.
too young to understand the actions of others.
emotionally overwhelmed by common painful sights.
pub.passage: The occasional sense of our being too weak for the ordinary incidents of life, is strangely distressing. The cry of an infant makes us wretched for hours after, in spite of every effort of reason. I saw, through my telescope, two big boys worrying a little one, and I could not look to see the end of it. They were so far off that there was nothing to be done. The distress to me was such--the picture of the lives of the three boys was so vivid--that I felt as if I had no reason nor courage left.
pub.question: As used in the text, the phrase “too weak for the ordinary incidents of life” most nearly suggests feeling

pub.explanation: 바로 앞 문장에서 거래가 시들해졌다고 하므로 이 구절은 금이 아주 조금씩만 들어오는 상황을 나타낸다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 정반대의 의미이고, C의 녹인 금과 D의 숨겨둔 금은 문맥과 관련이 없다.
pub.explanation_en: The preceding sentence says that trade had dried up, so this phrase describes a situation in which gold came in only in very small amounts. Therefore, the answer is A. B means the opposite, and the melted gold in C and the hidden gold in D have nothing to do with the context.
options: a very small, irregular trickle of gold coming in
a sudden flood of gold arriving all at once
a quantity of gold that had been melted down
a store of gold that was being secretly hidden
pub.passage:
A penny, worth fifty times as much as a sovereign, was something to retain and treasure. Doubtless, in their jungle-lairs, the wise old gray-beards put their heads together and agreed to raise the price on pennies when the worthless gold was all worked off. Who could tell? Mayhap the strange white men could be made to give even twenty sticks for a priceless copper.

By the end of the week the trade went slack. There was only the slightest dribble of gold. An occasional penny was reluctantly disposed of for ten sticks, while several thousand dollars in silver came in.

On the morning of the eighth day no trading was done. The gray-beards had matured their plan and were demanding twenty sticks for a penny, One-Eye delivered the new rate of exchange.

pub.explanation: 지문은 의식이 끝난 뒤 자매들의 위로와 아이 돌보기·가벼운 일로 이루어진 새 생활을 설명한다. 이어 'My situation was easy'라고 말한 뒤 'But still'로 전환하며 가족에 대한 기억이 행복을 앗아 갔다고 밝힌다. 따라서 D가 정답이다. 탈출·복수·사냥 찬양은 지문에 없으므로 A, B, C는 틀리다.
pub.explanation_en: The text describes a new life made up of the comfort of her sisters after the ceremony ended, along with looking after a child and doing light chores. After saying 'My situation was easy,' it turns with 'But still' and reveals that memories of her family took away her happiness. Therefore, the answer is D. A, B, and C are wrong because escape, revenge, and praise of the hunters do not appear in the text.
options: It lists the narrator's daily chores and then explains how she escaped from captivity.
It describes a harsh punishment and then the narrator's secret plan to seek revenge.
It praises the hunters' great skill and then describes one hunt the narrator joined.
It describes the narrator's easy new routine and then reveals her lasting sorrow.
pub.passage:
I was, however, happily disappointed, when at the close of the ceremony the company retired, and my sisters went about employing every means for my consolation and comfort.

Being now settled and provided with a home, I was employed in nursing the children, and doing light work about the house. Occasionally I was sent out with the Indian hunters, when they went but a short distance, to help them carry their game.

My situation was easy; I had no particular hardships to endure. But still, the recollection of my parents, my brothers and sisters, my home, and my own captivity, destroyed my happiness, and made me constantly solitary, lonesome and gloomy.

sourceText.author: Seaver, James E. (James Everett)
sourceText.work: A Narrative of the Life of Mrs. Mary Jemison

pub.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?

pub.explanation: 화자는 보험업을 '가장 고귀한 분야'라 부르며 지나치게 열광한다. 그러나 장애인을 '광고'로 본다거나 시와 정치에 더는 관심이 없다고 말하는 대목에서 그 열광이 우스꽝스럽게 편협함이 드러난다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A의 마지못한 수용, C의 후회, D의 진심 어린 동정은 모두 지문의 어조와 맞지 않는다.
pub.explanation_en: The narrator calls the insurance business 'the noblest field' and is excessively enthusiastic about it. But in the parts where he regards disabled people as 'advertisements' and says he no longer cares about poetry and politics, the enthusiasm shows itself to be comically narrow. Therefore, the answer is B. The reluctant acceptance in A, the regret in C, and the sincere sympathy in D all fail to match the tone of the text.
options: Reluctant acceptance of a dull but necessary occupation
Exaggerated enthusiasm that reveals a comically narrow outlook
Quiet regret about having given up his former love of poetry and politics
Sincere sympathy for the people injured in accidents
pub.passage: Certainly there is no nobler field for human effort than the insurance line of business--especially accident insurance. Ever since I have been a director in an accident-insurance company I have felt that I am a better man. Life has seemed more precious. Accidents have assumed a kindlier aspect. Distressing special providences have lost half their horror. I look upon a cripple now with affectionate interest--as an advertisement. I do not seem to care for poetry any more. I do not care for politics--even agriculture does not excite me.
pub.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward accident insurance?

pub.explanation: 'frightened rabbit'는 겁에 질려 이리저리 급히 달아나는 모습을 비유한다. 앞에서 그가 몸을 비틀고 피하려 해도 돼지에 계속 쫓긴다고 묘사되어 있다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 계획성을, C는 즐거움을, D는 가만히 기다림을 말해 지문의 다급한 도주와 맞지 않는다.
pub.explanation_en: 'Frightened rabbit' is a metaphor for fleeing in a hurried, terrified, zigzag way. The text earlier describes him twisting and trying to dodge but still being chased by the pig. Therefore, the answer is A. B suggests planning, C enjoyment, and D quiet waiting, none of which fits the passage's frantic flight.
options: moved in a hurried, panicked way to escape his pursuers
carefully planned a clever route to a safe hiding place
enjoyed the lively game as much as the crowd did
waited quietly among the trees until the crowd tired
pub.passage:
When Sepeli dropped both pig and Chancellor, a talking man from the windward coast picked up the carcass. Cornelius was on his feet and running, when the pig caught him on the legs and tripped him. The people and the army, with shouts and laughter, joined in the sport.

Twist and dodge as he would, everywhere the ex-Chancellor of the Exchequer was met or overtaken by the flying pig. He scuttled like a frightened rabbit in and out among the avocados and the palms. No hand was laid upon him, and his tormentors made way before him, but ever they pursued, and ever the pig flew as fast as hands could pick it up.

pub.explanation: 구절 바로 뒤에 이 책이 두 세기 반이 지난 뒤에도 '영구적인 영향력'을 행사한다는 설명이 이어진다. 따라서 '살아 있다'는 말은 책이 여전히 읽히고 영향력을 가진다는 뜻이므로 D가 정답이다. A는 이 책이 격언과 인물 묘사로 이루어졌다는 설명과 맞지 않는다. B는 '살아 있음'을 작가의 생애로 오해했고, C의 재발견은 언급되지 않는다.
pub.explanation_en: Right after the phrase, the text explains that the book still exerts 'permanent influence' two and a half centuries later. So 'alive' means the book is still read and influential, and the answer is D. A does not fit the description of the book as made up of maxims and character sketches. B misreads 'alive' as referring to the author's life, and C's rediscovery is never mentioned.
options: is filled with vivid scenes of physical action
describes its author's long and healthy life
was recently rediscovered after being lost
continues to be widely read and influential
pub.passage: One last word about our amiable author. His great book remains eminently alive, and wields after two centuries and a half a permanent influence. When you refer to it, you must not expect a logical development of philosophical theory. We do not look to find a system in a book of maxims and portraits. La Bruyere was a moralist, pure and simple; he awakened sensibility, he encouraged refinement, and he exposed the vicious difference which existed around him--and which no one else had seemed to notice--that the possession of more or fewer pieces of money made between human beings otherwise equal.

sourceText.author: Gosse, Edmund
sourceText.work: Three French Moralists and The Gallantry of France

pub.explanation: 글쓴이는 과학이 인구를 늘린 것은 작은 승리일 뿐이며 선악과 현명함의 비율은 그대로라고 말한다. 그런데도 물질적 화려함에서 인류의 진보를 결론짓는 것을 '말로 스스로를 속인다'고 표현한다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A의 약속 위반, C의 어휘 부족, D의 말다툼은 이 비유의 의미가 아니다.
pub.explanation_en: The writer says that science increasing the population is only a small victory, and that the proportion of good to evil and of wisdom is unchanged. Even so, concluding that humanity has progressed from material splendor is described as 'we cheat ourselves with words.' Therefore, the answer is B. The broken promises in A, the lack of vocabulary in C, and the quarrels in D are not what this figure of speech means.
options: break the promises and agreements they have made with one another
deceive themselves by using flattering language about progress
lack the vocabulary to describe scientific discovery
argue too often about the meaning of words
pub.passage:
Progress there is in knowledge; and science has enabled the number of human beings capable of existing upon this earth to be indefinitely multiplied. But this is but a small triumph if the ratio of the good and bad, the wise and the foolish, the full and the hungry, remains unaffected. And we cheat ourselves with words when we conclude out of our material splendour an advance of the race.

In two things there is progress--progress in knowledge of the outward world, and progress in material wealth. This last, for the present, creates, perhaps, more evils than it relieves; but suppose this difficulty solved--suppose the wealth distributed, and every peasant living like a peer--what then?

pub.explanation: 지문은 가파른 절벽, 울창한 숲, 좁은 길 하나 때문에 병사들이 한 줄로 천천히 다가와야 했고 멀리서도 쉽게 보였다고 설명한다. 이런 특징은 모두 공격을 막는 데 유리하므로, 정착지는 방어를 위해 선택되었다는 C가 정답이다. A는 고립된 지형이 이웃 마을과의 교역을 오히려 어렵게 만드므로 틀렸다. B는 절벽과 숲이 대규모 농장에 맞지 않고 지문에 농업 이야기가 없으므로 틀렸다. D는 산속 지형이 바다로 오는 방문객과 관련이 없고, 지문은 사람들을 막는 것에 초점을 두므로 틀렸다.
pub.explanation_en: The passage says the site had steep cliffs, thick forest, and only one narrow trail, so soldiers had to come slowly in single file and could be spotted from far away. All of these features help people protect themselves, so C is correct: the founders picked the site for defense. A is wrong because an isolated site would make trade with colonial towns harder, not easier. B is wrong because cliffs and forest don't suit large plantations, and the passage never mentions farming. D is wrong because a mountain site has nothing to do with visitors arriving by sea, and the passage is about keeping people out.
options: make it easier to trade crops with nearby colonial towns.
make it easier to grow large plantations of sugarcane.
make it easier to defend themselves against attackers.
make it easier to welcome visitors arriving by sea.
pub.passage: Maroon communities were settlements founded by people who escaped slavery in the Americas between the 1500s and the 1800s. Historians studying one maroon community in the mountains of Jamaica have found that its founders chose a site surrounded by steep cliffs and thick forest, reachable only by a single narrow trail. Colonial soldiers sent to recapture the residents could approach only in a slow single-file line, which made them easy to spot from far away. Because of these features, historians conclude that the founders most likely picked the location in order to ______

advisory.note: 단서가 직접 드러나 있고 추론은 한 단계뿐이다. 오답들은 쉽게 배제되지만 지나치게 엉뚱하지는 않다. B는 카리브해 지역의 사탕수수 맥락 때문에 어느 정도 그럴듯하게 보인다. 사소한 점: A의 'crops'는 B의 농업 주제와 겹치지만 문제는 되지 않는다.

pub.explanation: 'creep in'은 조용히 조금씩 스며드는 모습을 비유한다. 앞에서 화자는 자신이 'faltered'했다고 하고, 뒤에서는 그 사랑 때문에 결심이 약해져 더 이상 미워하지 않는다고 말한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 점진적 변화와 반대이고, C는 비유를 실제 침입으로 읽은 오류이며, D는 지문에 근거가 없다.
pub.explanation_en: 'Creep in' is a metaphor for something seeping in quietly, a little at a time. Earlier the speaker says he 'faltered', and later he says that love weakened his resolve so that he no longer hates. The answer is therefore A. B is the opposite of a gradual change, C is an error that reads the metaphor as an actual intrusion, and D has no basis in the text.
options: the speaker's feelings changed gradually, almost without notice
the speaker suddenly decided to forgive in a single moment
the speaker felt fear of someone sneaking into the house
the speaker tried hard to hide his love from others
pub.passage: I had faltered, and my cause was lost. What have I accomplished? Am I able to gloat over you? What have I wrought, after all? I weakened under the love she bore for you, I permitted it to creep in and fill my heart. Do you understand? I do not hate you now. It is something to know that you have worshipped her all these years. You were true to her. What you did long, long ago was not your fault. You believed that she had wronged you. But you went on loving her. That is what weakened my resolve. You loved her to the end, she loved you to the end. Well, in the face of that, could I go on hating you? You must have been worthy of her love.

pub.explanation: '아침'은 하루의 시작처럼 인생의 시작, 곧 어린 시절을 가리키는 비유다. 화자는 집을 '작은 낙원'이라 부르고 그 시절이 늘 생생하게 기억된다고 말한다. 따라서 C가 정답이다. A와 B는 '아침'을 글자 그대로 받아들였고, D의 시련은 그 시절 이후에 온 것이다.
pub.explanation_en: 'Morning' is a metaphor: like the start of the day, it refers to the start of life, that is, childhood. The narrator calls the house a 'little paradise' and says that time is always vividly remembered. The answer is therefore C. A and B take 'morning' literally, and the trials in D came after that period.
options: the early hours when the family began its daily work
a single morning the narrator remembers in detail
the early, joyful period of the narrator's life
a time of trial before the narrator reached old age
pub.passage:
During this period my mother had two sons, between whose ages there was a difference of about three years: the oldest was named Matthew, and the other Robert.

Health presided on every countenance, and vigor and strength characterized every exertion. Our mansion was a little paradise. The morning of my childish, happy days, will ever stand fresh in my remembrance, notwithstanding the many severe trials through which I have passed, in arriving at my present situation, at so advanced an age. Even at this remote period, the recollection of my pleasant home at my father's, of my parents, of my brothers and sister, and of the manner in which I was deprived of them all at once, affects me so powerfully, that I am almost overwhelmed with grief, that is seemingly insupportable.

sourceText.author: Seaver, James E. (James Everett)
sourceText.work: A Narrative of the Life of Mrs. Mary Jemison

pub.explanation: 'thunder-cloud'는 아직 터지지 않았지만 곧 쏟아질 듯한 위협을 비유한다. 앞 문장들에서 선원들이 투덜거리고 명령에 험악한 표정으로 마지못해 따른다고 하여 반란의 기운이 감돌고 있음을 보여 준다. 따라서 B가 정답이다. A는 반란이 이미 일어났다고 보아 틀리고, C는 비유를 실제 날씨로 읽은 오류이며, D는 지문에 근거가 없다.
pub.explanation_en: 'Thunder-cloud' is a metaphor for a threat that has not yet burst but seems about to pour down. The preceding sentences show the sailors grumbling and obeying orders reluctantly with sullen looks, indicating an atmosphere of mutiny. Therefore, the answer is B. A is wrong because it assumes the revolt has already happened, C reads the metaphor as actual weather, and D has no support in the text.
options: the crew had already openly seized control of the ship
a dangerous revolt seemed ready to break out at any moment
stormy weather was delaying the progress of the voyage
the sailors were grieving over companions lost at sea
pub.passage:
If the conduct of the men had been alarming in the boat, it became truly threatening when they had come aboard. They lay about the deck growling together in talk. The slightest order was received with a black look, and grudgingly and carelessly obeyed. Even the honest hands must have caught the infection, for there was not one man aboard to mend another. Mutiny, it was plain, hung over us like a thunder-cloud.

And it was not only we of the cabin party who perceived the danger. Long John was hard at work going from group to group, spending himself in good advice, and as for example no man could have shown a better.

sourceText.author: Stevenson, Robert Louis
sourceText.work: The Works of Robert Louis Stevenson - Swanston Edition, Vol. 06

pub.explanation: 필자는 그런 사람이 방에 들어오기만 해도 'insensibly we are conscious of a presence'라고 말한다. 반대로 영향력 없는 사람들은 'They never stir us'라고 대비되므로, 자기장 비유는 눈에 보이지 않지만 강하게 끌어당기는 존재감을 뜻한다. 따라서 A가 정답이다. B는 기온 비유를 신체적 불편으로 잘못 읽었고, C는 비유를 문자 그대로 받아들였으며, D는 끌림이 'charms us'일 수도 'repels'일 수도 있다는 내용과 맞지 않는다.
pub.explanation_en: The writer says that when such a person enters a room, "insensibly we are conscious of a presence." In contrast, people without influence are described as "They never stir us," so the magnetic-field metaphor means a presence that is invisible but pulls strongly. Therefore the answer is A. B misreads a temperature metaphor as physical discomfort, C takes the metaphor literally, and D does not match the statement that the attraction can "charm" us or "repel" us.
options: that such a person exerts a strong, invisible pull on everyone nearby.
that such a person makes others feel physically uncomfortable and hot.
that such a person works in a laboratory studying electricity and magnets.
that such a person forces others to agree with whatever is said aloud.
pub.passage:
Sometimes it charms us; sometimes it repels. But we can no more be oblivious to it than we can to the temperature of the air. Its possessor has but to enter the room, and insensibly we are conscious of a presence. It is as if we had suddenly been placed in the field of a magnetic force.

On the other hand there are people who produce no effect upon us whatever. They come and go with a like indifference. They are as unimportant psychically as if they were any other portion of the furniture. They never stir us. We might live with them for fifty years and be hardly able to tell, for any influence upon ourselves, whether they existed or not.

sourceText.author: Lowell, Percival
sourceText.work: The Soul of the Far East

pub.explanation: 전반부는 계단을 올라 초인종을 누르고 수녀가 문을 열어 주는 과정을 담담하게 서술한다. 이후 낮고 애처로운 성가가 시작되자 필자는 음악의 '지나친 구슬픔'을 묘사할 수 없다고 말하며 깊이 감동한다. 따라서 담담한 서술에서 깊은 슬픔과 감동으로 바뀌는 D가 정답이다. A는 변화 방향이 반대이고, B의 분노와 C의 지루함은 지문에 없다.
pub.explanation_en: The first half calmly narrates climbing the stairs, ringing the bell, and a nun opening the door. When a low, plaintive chant then begins, the writer says the music's "excessive mournfulness" cannot be described and is deeply moved. So the answer is D, a shift from plain narration to deep sorrow and emotion. A has the direction of change reversed, and the anger in B and the boredom in C are not in the text.
options: From solemn grief to cheerful relief.
From eager curiosity to angry disapproval.
From familiar comfort to bored indifference.
From plain narration to deep, moved sorrow.
pub.passage: I mounted the steps, however, and rung at the door. It was opened by a pale nun, of thirty, who hesitated a moment, and let me pass. In a small, plain chapel within, the service of the altar was just commencing, and, before I reached a seat, a low plaintive chant commenced, in female voices from the choir. It went on with occasional interruptions from the prayers, for perhaps an hour. I can not describe the excessive mournfulness of the music. One or two familiar hymns occurred in the course of it, like airs in a recitative, the same sung in our churches, but the effect was totally different.

sourceText.author: Willis, Nathaniel Parker
sourceText.work: Pencillings by the Way Written During Some Years of Residence and Travel in Europe

pub.explanation: 처음에 아이들은 결혼 놀이를 함께 하며 의식을 제대로 치른다. 그러나 아기 역할을 정하는 대목에서 Teresa와 Bob이 서로 원하지 않는 역할을 거부하며 다툰다. 따라서 협력하는 놀이에서 사소한 말다툼으로 바뀌는 B가 정답이다.
pub.explanation_en: At first, the children play wedding together and carry out the ceremony properly. But when they assign the role of the baby, Teresa and Bob quarrel, each refusing the role the other wants. Therefore, the answer is B, a shift from cooperative play to petty arguing.
options: from a bitter quarrel to friendly agreement
from cooperative play to petty arguing
from timid fear to growing bravery
from a solemn ritual to shared grief
pub.passage:
ELSIE.

No, that's too rough. We'll play husband and wife. Bob and I will get married, and, Teresa, you must be the minister and a bridesmaid.

(_They retire into the house, where, with the aid of a wrapper, a night dress, a bouquet, and a black mackintosh, the ceremony is properly performed._)

ELSIE.

Now we'll have a little girl baby, and (_to Teresa_) you must be it.

TERESA.

No, I want to be the wife now, and you be the baby.

ELSIE.

No, I'll be the husband, and let Bob be the baby.

BOB.

I won't be the baby!
pub.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?

pub.explanation: 처음에 그녀는 'a slight laugh and a smile'을 띠고 가볍게 돌로 다가간다. 그러나 돌이 꿈쩍도 하지 않자 군중이 신음하고 그녀는 비명과 함께 쓰러진다. 따라서 가벼운 자신감에서 낙담으로 바뀌는 C가 정답이다. A와 B는 방향이 반대이고, D의 분노와 체념은 지문에 없다.
pub.explanation_en: At first, she approaches the stone lightly with 'a slight laugh and a smile'. But when the stone does not budge at all, the crowd groans and she falls with a scream. Therefore, the answer is C, a shift from light confidence to dismay. A and B have the direction reversed, and the anger and resignation in D are not in the text.
options: It moves from fearful dread to relieved laughter as the crowd cheers.
It moves from solemn silence to playful teasing among the spectators.
It moves from light confidence to dismay as the stone refuses to move.
It moves from angry defiance to calm acceptance of the old legend.
pub.passage: There might have been a slight blush on her cheek at appearing before so many people on such an undertaking; but yet, with a slight laugh and a smile on her lips, she advanced towards the stone. There was a perfect silence among the crowd of spectators as she touched the stone. It did not move. Again and again she touched it, with all the force she could exert. The stone remained as immovable as if part of the mass on which it rested. There was a general groan uttered by the crowd, an evidence of their full belief in the truth of the legend, while, at the same moment, a piercing cry was heard, and the unhappy damsel was seen to fall fainting to the ground.
pub.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?

pub.explanation: 첫 연은 영광의 무덤에 노인의 재가 누워 있다는 엄숙한 장면으로 시작한다. 마지막 부분에서 젊은이는 눈물 젖은 눈들을 보고 노인이 '하늘 너머에서 용서받았다'는 위안으로 나아가므로 D가 정답이다. A는 비난이 없어 틀렸고, B의 분노한 항의와 C의 장난스러운 재치는 지문의 엄숙한 어조와 맞지 않는다.
pub.explanation_en: The first stanza begins with a solemn scene in which an old man's ashes lie in a tomb of glory. In the last part, the young man sees the tear-filled eyes and moves toward the comfort that the old man has been 'forgiven beyond the heavens,' so D is the answer. A is wrong because there is no condemnation, and the angry protest of B and the playful wit of C do not match the solemn tone of the text.
options: From cheerful praise to bitter condemnation.
From angry protest to resigned silence.
From playful wit to anxious, growing dread.
From somber reflection to consoling reassurance.
pub.passage:
Low in the tomb of glory
The old man's ashes lie--
Unuttered this my story,
Unwritten to human eye;
And the young man, blessed and blessing,
Walks over the shady town,
The evil passions repressing,
And his head bent humbly down.

Perhaps he marvels why treasure
Of the judge to his credit is set,
And an old revival measure
Should have been the statesman's pet.
But he hears the invitation,
And sees the streaming eyes
Of the old man lost to the nation,
And forgiven beyond the skies.
pub.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?

pub.explanation: 처음에 서술자 일행은 총을 쏘아 원주민들을 'at a distance'에 두며 경계했다. 그러나 아침에 서술자는 선물을 들고 그들에게 갔고 그들이 'very friendly indeed'가 되었다고 기록한다. 따라서 경계에서 호의로 바뀐 A가 정답이다. 헤엄치지 못한 것은 원주민이 아니라 서술자 일행이므로 C는 틀리고, B와 D도 근거가 없다.
pub.explanation_en: At first, the narrator's party was wary and kept the natives 'at a distance' by firing guns. But in the morning the narrator went to them with gifts and recorded that they became 'very friendly indeed.' Therefore, A, which describes the shift from wariness to goodwill, is the answer. It was the narrator's party, not the natives, who could not swim, so C is wrong, and B and D have no support.
options: Friendly goodwill after an initially wary start
Lasting distrust despite the exchange of gifts
Amused scorn for their inability to cross water
Quiet indifference to their repeated invitations
pub.passage: Last night we heard the calls of natives at the opposite side of the river. As soon as they saw us, they crossed the river, and came pretty close to us: the discharge of our guns, however, kept them at a distance. Several of our party, during their watches saw them moving with fire sticks on the other side of the river. In the morning, three of them came boldly up; so I went to them with some presents, and they became very friendly indeed. Presents were exchanged; and they invited us in the most pressing manner to accompany them to their camp; and were evidently disappointed in finding that we could not swim.

sourceText.author: Leichhardt, Ludwig
sourceText.work: Journal of an Overland Expedition in Australia From Moreton Bay to Port Essington, a distance of upwards of 3000 miles, during the years 1844-1845
